sentences.text: This tiny dinosaur measured roughly 60 centimeters in length and had a mass of about 0.82 kilograms.
Its leg bone was significantly longer than its arm bone, measuring 84 millimeters compared to 71 millimeters.
Feathers covered the head, body, forelimbs, and hind limbs.
It possessed a dentary tooth count probably lower than 10 and teeth similar in morphology to those of basal birds.
At just 60 centimeters long and weighing 0.82 kilograms, it was one of the smallest known dinosaurs.
Its leg bone was significantly longer than its arm bone, measuring 84 millimeters compared to 71 millimeters.
Feathers covered the head, body, forelimbs, and hind limbs.
The holotype skeleton was likely collected in the Linglongta area of Jianchang from the Tiaojishan Formation.
Xiaotingia was first named and classified by Xing Xu, Hailu You, Kai Du, and Fenglu Han in 2011.
The type species, Xiaotingia zhengi, honors the paleontologist Zheng Xiaoting.
Xiaotingia was a small feathered dinosaur that inhabited an arboreal environment.
Researchers suggest the limb proportions might indicate it stood on hind limbs and could flap forelimbs to achieve flight.
If it could fly short distances, it might have also used its hind limbs as wings.
It is classified within the family Anchiornithidae.
It is a genus of theropod ceratosaurian dinosaur.
Xiaotingia lived in western Liaoning, China, during the Middle Jurassic or early Late Jurassic.
The animal lived between approximately 165 and 153 million years ago, spanning the Bathonian and Oxfordian stages.
A later analysis challenged the initial hypothesis, recovering Archaeopteryx as an avialan while placing Xiaotingia closely allied to Anchiornis within the Troodontidae.
However, a more exhaustive analysis published months later questioned this, finding Archaeopteryx as an avialan again while Xiaotingia remained closely related to Anchiornis within Troodontidae.
However, in 2012 new revisions suggested Xiaotingia was a basal dromaeosaurid, not a troodontid.
A 2017 study re-examining the 'Harlem specimen' of Archaeopteryx concluded that Xiaotingia would belong to another family, the anchiornithids.
